Contemplative

/kun-TEM-pluh-tiv/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Contemplative means involved in or characterized by deep, calm, unhurried thought or reflection.

Contemplative means involved in or characterized by deep, calm, unhurried thought or reflection. The garden was designed for contemplative walks, its gravel paths looping slowly past a single stone basin.

Worked Example

Every January, the violin maker closed his shop for a week — not to travel, but to sit with the year's unfinished instruments. He would hold each one, turn it in the window light, and jot a line or two in a notebook, sometimes an hour apart. Apprentices learned not to mistake the stillness for idleness. That contemplative week, he insisted, saved him from a year of hurried mistakes.

A week of slow, deliberate reflection — holding, watching, noting a line an hour — is the calm, unhurried deep thought that contemplative describes.

How Contemplative Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

reflective

reflective: given to careful thought

meditative

meditative: calmly absorbed in inward attention

Antonyms

impulsive

impulsive: acting without thinking

rash

rash: hasty and careless

How Strong Is It? — thoughtful → monastic → contemplative

thoughtful vs. contemplative

thoughtful vs. contemplative: Thoughtful is weaker than contemplative: a thoughtful person considers things carefully, while a contemplative one builds real stretches of unhurried reflection into life itself.

monastic vs. contemplative

monastic vs. contemplative: Monastic is stronger than contemplative — a monastic life is structured entirely around silence and reflection, while contemplative can describe a single quiet walk.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — con-

Prefix — con-: with; intently

Root — templ

Root — templ: a space marked out for observation (Latin templum)

Suffix — -ative

Suffix — -ative: tending to; having the nature of

Put it together

Put it together: Contemplative hides a lovely picture: Latin templum was the space a Roman augur marked out in the sky to watch for omens — patient, careful observation in a dedicated space. Contemplari meant 'to observe intently,' and with the suffix -ative the word becomes 'characterized by intent, unhurried observation.' The same templum gives temple (a marked-out sacred space) and template (a marked-out shape) — three rooms built from one floor plan.

Use the root in a new word: template

Use the root in a new word: template: A template marks out the shape to follow — from templum, the marked-out space where Roman augurs did their careful sky-watching, the same watchful root behind contemplative study.

Word Choice

formal to literary; calm and approving

Contemplative names calm, unhurried, deep reflection — more neutral and peaceful than this unit's pensive, whose thought carries a wistful, melancholy shade, and nothing like impassive, which describes an unreadable, unemotional exterior rather than a thinking state.
